summary: Defines the UPDATE method for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). It lets a client change session parameters, such as media streams and codecs, without affecting the dialog state. Unlike a re-INVITE, it can be sent before the initial INVITE has finished, which suits early dialogs.

eli5.summary: Imagine changing your mind about what to order while the call is still ringing. UPDATE lets a phone adjust the call's settings before the other person has even picked up.

subtitle: A SIP request that changes a session's media settings without touching the dialog, even before the call is answered.

tldr.problem: A SIP re-INVITE changes both the session and the dialog state, so it cannot be used to change media settings (for example putting early media on hold) before the initial INVITE has been answered.
tldr.mechanism: The UPDATE method carries an SDP offer inside an existing dialog, early or confirmed, and the answer comes back in the 2xx response to the UPDATE. It has no effect on dialog state.
tldr.outcome: Either side can adjust session parameters while the call is still ringing. On confirmed dialogs the RFC still recommends a re-INVITE, because UPDATE must be answered immediately.

facts.label: Retry timer after 491
facts.value: 2.1 to 4 s (Call-ID owner), 0 to 2 s (other side)

today: RFC 3311 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the SIP UPDATE method.

sections.title: Why a New Method Was Needed
sections.content:
The SIP INVITE method affects two pieces of state at once: the session (the media streams that SIP sets up) and the dialog (the state SIP itself defines). Usually that is fine, but the coupling causes trouble when the session must change before the initial INVITE has been answered.

The RFC's example is early media: a session set up to convey call progress before the INVITE is accepted. Either side should be able to change it, for example by putting the early media on hold, but a re-INVITE also affects the dialog, so it cannot be used. UPDATE fills that gap. A user agent can send it within a dialog, early or confirmed, to update session parameters without changing dialog state.
sections.eli5: A re-INVITE is like rewriting the whole phone call plan. UPDATE only tweaks the volume knob, so you can do it while the phone is still ringing.

sections.title: How UPDATE Works
sections.content:
The caller starts an INVITE transaction as normal. Once a dialog exists, early or confirmed, the caller can send an UPDATE that contains an SDP offer. The answer travels in the response to the UPDATE. The callee can do the same: it sends an UPDATE with an offer, and the caller puts its answer in the 2xx response to that UPDATE.

The Allow header field signals support for the method. Extra limits on when an UPDATE can be sent come from the restrictions of the offer/answer model.
sections.eli5: One side says 'can we change to this setting?' and the other side answers 'yes' in its reply. Either side is allowed to ask.

sections.title: Finding Out if the Other Side Supports UPDATE
sections.content:
A compliant UAC SHOULD include an Allow header field listing UPDATE in its INVITE. A compliant UAS that sends a reliable provisional response containing SDP SHOULD list UPDATE in that response's Allow header field. An unreliable provisional response MAY list it, and a 2xx response SHOULD.

If a response carries an Allow header field containing UPDATE, the UAC knows the callee supports it and may follow the sending procedures. A reliable provisional response always creates an early dialog at the UAC, which is needed in order to receive UPDATE requests from the callee.
sections.eli5: Before asking for a change, you check whether the other phone says 'I understand UPDATE' on its list of things it can do.

sections.title: Sending, Receiving and Answering an UPDATE
sections.content:
An UPDATE is built like any other in-dialog request. It MAY be sent in early or confirmed dialogs, by caller or callee. On a confirmed dialog a re-INVITE is RECOMMENDED instead, because an UPDATE must be answered immediately, which rules out asking the user for approval.

UPDATE is a target refresh request, so it can change the remote target of a dialog. The offer/answer rules of RFC 3261 still apply: a side cannot send an UPDATE with an offer while an earlier offer of its own is unanswered, or while an offer it received is unanswered.

On receipt, a UAS has these rules:

  • An UPDATE arriving before a final response to a previous UPDATE on the same dialog gets a 500 with a Retry-After value chosen randomly between 0 and 10 seconds.
  • An UPDATE with an offer when the UAS has an unanswered offer of its own gets a 491.
  • An UPDATE with an offer when the UAS has not yet answered an offer it received gets a 500 with Retry-After.
  • If the session description changed and the change cannot be made without prompting the user, the UAS SHOULD reject with 504. An unacceptable description can be rejected with 488.

If the UAC gets a non-2xx final response, the session parameters stay unchanged. A 491 response makes the UAC SHOULD start a timer: 2.1 to 4 seconds if it owns the Call-ID, or 0 to 2 seconds if not, in units of 10 ms. Then it tries once more if it still wants the change.
sections.eli5: If two people ask for a change at the same moment, one is told 'wait a moment and ask again', and each waits a different random time so they do not collide again.

sections.title: Example Call Flow
sections.content:
The RFC's example starts with an INVITE carrying an offer. The callee answers with a 180 that includes the answer, so the session is established while the dialog is still early. The caller sends PRACK and gets a 200. The caller then sends an UPDATE with a new offer, for example to put the session on hold, and gets the answer in the 200 to the UPDATE.

Shortly after, the callee sends its own UPDATE with an offer, and the caller answers in the 200. Finally the callee answers the call with a 200 to the INVITE and the caller sends an ACK. Neither the 200 nor the ACK contains SDP.
sections.eli5: Both people change the call settings a couple of times while the phone is still ringing, and only then does the other person pick up.

sections.title: Proxies, Security and IANA
sections.content:
Proxies treat UPDATE like any other non-INVITE request. The security considerations are identical to those for re-INVITE: an UPDATE should be integrity protected and authenticated as coming from the same source as the entity on the other end of the dialog. RFC 3261 discusses mechanisms for this.

The RFC also registers the UPDATE request method with IANA, per Section 27.4 of RFC 3261. The BNF for Method gains an UPDATEm alternative.
sections.eli5: You must make sure the change request really comes from the person you are talking to, not from a stranger.
